newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Contact Group urges Milosevic to accept democracy.
newsitem.headline: Contact Group urges Milosevic to accept democracy.

text.p: A senior U.S. government official urged Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday to give in to democratic pressures as anti-government protests in Belgrade entered a fifth week.

"There was a general consensus that there is a political crisis in Serbia, that reform is necessary," John Kornblum, Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs, told reporters in Geneva after a meeting of the five-nation Contact Group on former Yugoslavia.
"Milosevic has to yield to democratic pressures and tendencies and to open up and reform his system," said Kornblum, who met Serbian opposition figures in Geneva on Sunday.
In Brussels, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Monday the international community must keep pressure on Milosevic to recognise an election victory by opposition parties in his country.
"We believe that these election results should be honoured," he told reporters. "Subverting democratic election processes is an action which the United States cannot support."

Carl Bildt, international High Representative to Bosnia who also attended Monday's Contact Group meeting in Geneva, said: "What we see in the streets of Belgrade today, which is encouraging, shows the beginnings of the democratic process in Serbia."
"All members of the Contact Group have made clear their support for the democractic process in Serbia."
Kornblum met Bosnian Serb opposition leader Vuk Draskovic and other members of the Zajedno (Together) coalition in Geneva and urged Milosevic to accept the results of the election.
Draskovic, who heads the Serb Renewal Movement, said he was seeking diplomatic support from the United States and European Union and accused Milosevic of provoking violence and civil war.
Police have so far kept a low profile during the rallies, in contrast to 1991 when Milosevic used tanks to crush the last big street challenge.
